optionalSupplies: Reflective vest or strip you already own
substitutes: No dog light? Use reflective tape on your own jacket and a steady flashlight pointed down.
No flashlight? Use your phone light, low and pointed at the ground.
variations: Porch version: sit on your doorstep or at the window with the lights-out minute only, if the dog does not feel like a walk.
Short version: one lantern stop just outside your door, then home.
Gentle version for a senior dog: stay on a flat, very familiar route with an extra bench stop and cut it short if they slow.

Star minute: on a clear evening, make the lights-out minute a star minute. Find the moon or a bright planet and one bright star, join three or four stars into a constellation named after your dog, and say its name once, softly, before heading in.
title: The Dusk Lantern Stroll
clue: The streetlights come on, and your whole route is one pool of light after another.
reveal: A slow walk at the turn of the day, from one pool of lamplight to the next. You and your dog both wear a soft light, stop at three light pools of your choice, and share a minute of lights-out listening before heading home.
objective: Walk a short, familiar dusk route with soft visibility lights, pausing at lamp pools for sniffs and a lights-out minute, then hang the light up at home.
instructions: In the afternoon, set out your lantern kit: a soft, steady clip-on LED light for your dog's harness, a small flashlight or headlamp for you, and anything reflective you already own. Skip candles, flames, sparklers and glow sticks. Keep batteries and small parts where your dog cannot reach them.

Try the dog's light indoors first. Let your dog look and sniff, clip it on only if they seem fine, and watch for scratching or fussing. Choose a steady light over a flashing one and keep it out of their eyes. If they dislike it, use your own light and reflective items only.
Pick a short, familiar, well-lit route and set off just before dusk. Choose three lamp pools along the way as your lanterns, such as a lamp post, a lit gate or a shop window.
Walk on a short leash near roads and let your dog set the pace. Point your own flashlight at the ground ahead, never toward your dog's face or a driver.
At each lantern stop, pause in the glow, stand still and let your dog sniff for as long as they like. There is no destination and no timer at a lantern.
Between lamps, walk the dark stretch slowly. Keep to the edge, listen for bikes and cars and keep your dog close and move away from any wildlife you spot, such as a fox.

At a quiet spot away from the road, such as your own front step or a bench, switch off your own flashlight for the lights-out minute. Leave your dog's light on, stand or sit still, and listen to the evening together.
At home, switch off your dog's light, check the harness and paws, and hang the light on its hook. The lantern goes home. Offer water and let them settle.
twist: The route is made of light pools rather than distance: you only count the lamps you stopped at, and the finale is a minute with your own light off.
completion: You have stopped at one lamp pool, shared the lights-out minute (or its porch version) and hung the light up at home.
photoIdea: Your dog's paws and a pool of lamplight on the sidewalk from behind, with the clip light glowing softly in the frame.
memoryPrompt: Which lamp stop did your dog like most, and what was the evening sound during the lights-out minute?
supplies: Leash and a harness your dog already wears
A soft clip-on LED light for the harness, or a small flashlight
safety: Use a steady clip-on light only (no flames or glow sticks) with the battery case closed.
Skip fireworks and bonfire evenings, keep your dog on a leash, and stay on lit sidewalks and stop at crossings.
Hand-test warm sidewalks, wipe paws after de-icer or salt, and skip the walk in extreme weather.
